title: Anomalously high quasiparticle thermal conductivity in the underdoped cuprate superconductor HgBa$_{2}$CuO$_{4+δ}$
authors: Jordan Baglo, Quentin Barthélemy, Étienne Lefrançois, Anne Forget, Dorothée Colson, Cyril Proust, Louis Taillefer
abstract: The single-layer cuprate superconductor HgBa$_{2}$CuO$_{4+δ}$ (Hg1201) is an ideal candidate for investigating many properties of cuprates with minimal disorder and without the complication of multiple CuO$_2$ layers. Here we measure the in-plane longitudinal thermal conductivity $κ$ of underdoped Hg1201 ($T_c$ = 76 K, $p$ = 0.11) at dilution refrigerator temperatures to extract the nodal quasiparticle velocity ratio $v_F/v_Δ$. Assuming contributions from only a single line node per quadrant on the Fermi surface leads to a value of $v_F/v_Δ$ = $23 \pm 3$, anomalously large compared to other cuprates at similar dopings. In conjunction with the anomalously high quasiparticle specific heat of Hg1201 in the normal state reported previously at a similar doping, this points to more than one Fermi surface sheet crossing the nodal line, suggesting the presence of more than the single small electron pocket detected by quantum oscillations.
summary: This work measures the low-temperature thermal conductivity in the underdoped cuprate $	ext{HgBa}_2	ext{CuO}_{4+\delta}$ to probe its nodal quasiparticle structure. By analyzing the field dependence of the residual thermal conductivity, the authors extract a large velocity ratio ($v_F/v_\Delta$). This result strongly suggests that the Fermi surface is more complex than previously assumed, likely involving multiple electronic pockets contributing to the heat transport.
main_problem: To investigate anomalous properties of high-Tc cuprate superconductors, specifically determining the nodal quasiparticle velocity ratio ($v_F / v_\Delta$) using thermal conductivity measurements.
main_result: The measured residual linear thermal conductivity ($\kappa_0/T$) yields an anomalously large quasiparticle velocity ratio ($v_F / v_\Delta = 23 \pm 3$), suggesting the presence of more than one Fermi surface sheet crossing the nodal line.
method: Measuring in-plane longitudinal thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) at very low temperatures and extrapolating the field dependence using the K¨ubert-Hirschfeld model to extract the zero-field residual term $\kappa_0/T$.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the single-layer cuprate superconductor $	ext{HgBa}_2	ext{CuO}_{4+\delta}$ ($	ext{Hg1201}$). The analysis uses theoretical models for nodal d-wave superconductors relating $\kappa_0/T$ to the ratio of Fermi and gap velocities.
key_observables: In-plane longitudinal thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), the residual linear term $\kappa_0(B)/T$, and the velocity ratio $v_F / v_\Delta$.
important_parameters: $T_c = 76 	ext{ K}$, doping $p = 0.11$, low temperatures (down to $0.1 	ext{ K}$), magnetic field dependence ($B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes contributions from only a single line node per quadrant when calculating the velocity ratio, though this assumption is challenged by other experimental results.
figures_summary: Figures show $\kappa/T$ vs. $T$ at various magnetic fields, and the extrapolation of $\kappa_0(B)/T$ vs. $B$, which are fitted to theoretical models.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and measurement technique (thermal conductivity). It applies a theoretical model relating $\kappa_0/T$ to nodal properties, derives an anomalously large velocity ratio from the data, and concludes by suggesting that this implies multiple Fermi surface sheets are present in the material.
why_interesting: The investigation of thermal transport provides a highly sensitive probe into the gap structure and electronic dimensionality of strongly correlated materials like cuprates, offering insights complementary to ARPES or quantum oscillation measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Low temperature thermal conductivity of Hg1201 at p = 0.11 measured at several magnetic field values as indicated, plotted as κ/T vs T. The observed linear low- temperature behavior is used to extrapolate to T = 0 (solid lines) to provide the κ0(B)/T data shown in Fig. 2.

FIG. 2. Extrapolated T →0 thermal conductivity data κ0(B)/T resulting from the fits in Fig. 1, plotted as κ0/T vs B. The solid line is a fit to the K¨ubert-Hirschfeld model [27] (Eq. 2). The resulting extrapolation to B = 0 gives κ0/T = 14 ± 2 mW/K2m (this error includes the uncertainty in sam- ple geometry).
